subject: ba
title: Forms of Business Combinations
objectives: Define the concept and motivations behind business combinations.
Distinguish between mergers, acquisitions, absorption and consolidation.
Analyse the differences between horizontal, vertical and conglomerate combinations.
Evaluate the strategic implications of hostile versus friendly takeovers.
study:
A business combination brings two or more previously independent firms under common control. The core motive is synergy — the idea that the combined entity is worth more than the sum of its parts, expressed as 1+1>2. Combinations are generally grouped by the relationship between the firms involved: horizontal, vertical, or conglomerate.

Key termMerger — a transaction where an acquiring company takes over a target company as a whole, leaving only one company remaining afterward.

A merger is a fusion of two companies into one; an acquisition (takeover) is the purchase of a target company's shares by an acquirer, who may keep or dissolve the target as a separate entity. In a consolidation, both original companies disappear entirely and a brand-new third company is formed. In an absorption, a larger, dominant firm simply swallows a smaller one, which loses its identity completely.

Horizontal integration combines competitors in the same industry (two banks merging, or two soft-drink companies). Vertical integration combines firms at different stages of the same production chain — backward integration moves toward raw material sources (a bakery buying a flour mill), while forward integration moves toward the end consumer (a manufacturer buying a retail chain). A conglomerate combines completely unrelated businesses purely to diversify risk and spread revenue streams — a shipping company buying a hotel chain, for instance.

Exam tipDirection matters for vertical integration: "backward" always means toward suppliers/raw materials, "forward" always means toward distribution/the end consumer. Questions frequently test this with a concrete example rather than the term itself.

Takeovers can be friendly (approved by the target's board) or hostile (the acquirer buys shares directly from shareholders against target management's wishes). A strategic alliance differs from all of the above in that the companies involved remain independent — they cooperate without merging. Anti-trust law is most concerned with horizontal mergers specifically, since those are the ones most likely to create a monopoly and restrict competition.
recap:
• Synergy (1+1>2) is the core motive behind business combinations.
  • Merger = fusion into one; Acquisition = purchase of another company; Consolidation = both disappear, new company formed; Absorption = larger firm swallows smaller, which loses identity.
  • Horizontal = same industry/competitors; Vertical = different production stages (backward = toward suppliers, forward = toward consumers); Conglomerate = unrelated industries, for risk diversification.
  • Takeovers: friendly (board-approved) vs hostile (against management's wishes).
  • Strategic alliance: companies cooperate but remain independent — not a combination.
  • Anti-trust law focuses mainly on horizontal mergers, due to monopoly risk.
